v.why: Raising an already large learning rate makes Adam diverge, causing large accuracy drops (exps 4, 5, 7, 13).
At tiny learning rates the network is undertrained, so a step up gives consistent gains (exps 1, 14).
Deeper nets are less stable at high learning rates, so adding a layer then causes collapse (exps 85, 87).
With slow learning, the extra capacity of a deeper net helps it fit more within the epoch budget (exps 84, 86).
Raising an already strong L2 penalty pushes the model into underfitting (exps 64, 67, 71).
Larger batches reduce gradient noise and stabilize training at high learning rates (exp 48).
Small, noisy batches combined with many updates amplify the instability of a higher learning rate (exp 7).
Three-layer nets are the most sensitive to learning-rate increases (exps 12, 13).
The L2 penalty is applied per minibatch, so small batches magnify its effect (exps 71, 77).
Under strong L2 penalty, larger batches weaken the per-batch effective regularization and relieve underfitting (exp 54).

raw:
Main patterns in the 100 experiments:

- **Learning rate:** raising it helps when it starts low and collapses accuracy when it starts high. The collapse is worst with small batches and deep nets.
- **Depth:** adding a layer follows the same learning-rate dependence.
- **Alpha (L2 penalty):** raising it hurts most when it is already large or when batches are small. This is likely because the penalty is applied per minibatch.
